title: Why Most Enterprise AI Pilots Fail — and How the FDE Model Fixes It
excerpt: An analysis of why promising AI pilots stall before production, and how embedding engineers inside the client team closes the gap.
body:
A widely quoted figure says that the large majority of enterprise AI pilots never reach production. Whatever the exact number turns out to be for your organisation, the pattern is familiar: a convincing demo, an enthusiastic steering committee, and then months of silence while the pilot waits for integration, security review or an owner.

Where pilots actually stall

  • The handoff gap. A consulting team builds a prototype outside the client's environment. Rebuilding it inside real systems is a second project nobody budgeted for.
  • No business owner. The pilot is measured on model accuracy, not on a cost, revenue or efficiency outcome someone is accountable for.
  • Data reality. The demo used a clean extract. Production data is late, messy and governed by access rules.
  • Operational readiness. Monitoring, fallbacks, human review and support were treated as "later".

What changes with embedded engineering

In a Forward Deployed Engineering model, engineers work inside your repositories, your tooling and your sprint cadence from the first week. That removes the handoff: the prototype is built where it will run, against the systems it must integrate with, under the security rules that will apply in production.

A practical checklist

  1. Name one business owner and one measurable outcome before writing code.
  2. Agree the production environment and access path in week one.
  3. Plan monitoring, evaluation and human-in-the-loop review as part of the build, not after it.
  4. Ship a thin vertical slice to real users early, then widen it.

If you would like to talk through where an AI initiative of yours is stuck, get in touch.

title: The 12-Week AI Sprint: From Idea to Production
excerpt: A look at how an engagement moves from discovery to a production system in about twelve weeks, and what you receive at each stage.
body:
Long, open-ended consulting engagements are a common reason AI initiatives lose momentum. Our delivery model compresses the journey into phases with clear outputs, so you can see progress and decide at each stage whether to continue.

Discover (weeks 1–2)

AI maturity assessment, stakeholder interviews, a review of the data landscape and prioritisation of use cases. Output: an AI opportunity map and a prioritised use-case backlog.

Design (weeks 3–4)

Technical architecture, technology selection, a security and governance framework, team structure and a sprint-by-sprint build plan. Output: a technical blueprint and a security and governance framework.

Deploy (weeks 5–12)

Iterative build with embedded engineers, release to real users, and hardening for production: monitoring, evaluation and operational runbooks.

Scale (week 13 onward)

Extend to further use cases, teams or regions, and keep improving models and outcomes against the metrics agreed at the start.

Why it works

Each phase ends with a deliverable, a decision and a fixed next step. You are never committed to more than the next phase. The details of how we engage are on the engagement models page.

title: RAG vs. Fine-Tuning: Which LLM Approach Fits Your Enterprise Use Case?
excerpt: A practical framework for choosing between retrieval-augmented generation, fine-tuning, or a combination of both.
body:
Two techniques come up in almost every enterprise LLM project: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and fine-tuning. They solve different problems, and choosing the wrong one is an expensive mistake.

What each does

  • RAG gives a model access to your documents at question time. The model retrieves relevant passages and answers from them.
  • Fine-tuning changes the model's behaviour by training it further on examples: its tone, its output format, or how it handles a narrow task.

When RAG is usually the better fit

  • Your knowledge changes often (policies, product catalogues, tickets).
  • You need answers grounded in, and citing, specific source documents.
  • Different users must see different content, so access control matters.
  • You want to correct an answer by fixing a document rather than retraining.

When fine-tuning earns its cost

  • You need a consistent style or strict structured output.
  • A narrow, high-volume task where a smaller tuned model can cut latency and cost.
  • Behaviour that is hard to specify in a prompt but easy to show with examples.

Often the answer is both

A tuned model for format and tone, with RAG supplying current facts, is a common production pattern. Whatever you choose, build an evaluation set first. Without one you cannot tell whether a change helped.

If you are weighing options for a specific use case, talk to our team.
